I tried using the time series analysis library Prophet.
In the article above, I learned about a time series analysis library for Python and R called Prophet (Prophet?). It seems to be a widely used library.
Prophet is a forecasting procedure implemented in R and Python. It provides fast, fully automated forecasts and also allows data scientists and analysts to tune them manually.

Prophet is a procedure for forecasting time series data based on an additive model where non-linear trends are fit with yearly, weekly, and daily seasonality, plus holiday effects. It works best with time series that have strong seasonal effects and several seasons of historical data. Prophet is robust to missing data and shifts in the trend, and typically handles outliers well.
Let's just run it as shown on the official page. It seemed to work in Google Colab without needing to install Prophet.
from prophet import Prophet
df = pd.read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/facebook/prophet/main/examples/example_wp_log_peyton_manning.csv')
The input to Prophet is always a dataframe with two columns: ds (datestamp) and y, just like the dataframe above. The y column must be numeric and represent the measurement you want to forecast.
Now, let's use Prophet.
Next, we perform the forecast. Pass the future dataframe created earlier to the predict method.
forecast = m.predict(future)

The predict method assigns a predicted value to each row in future and names it yhat. If you pass past dates, it provides an in-sample fit. The forecast object here is a new dataframe. The dataframe contains the predicted yhat column, as well as columns for components and uncertainty intervals.
So, although I don't fully understand it yet, I took a look at the code on the official Prophet page since it's a library that's getting a lot of attention.
